objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the passenger briefing, checklist, navigation data and cargo rules at commercial depth, and teach a learner to brief passengers, secure the cabin, manage automation and devices, handle inoperative equipment and passenger distractions, and make sound SRM decisions, while you spot and fix the errors learners make.
why: Safe flight begins and ends on the ground, and hasty ground operations shrink the margin of safety [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. A major objective of primary training is to set habit patterns that last a whole career [[24:36|AFH 1-15]], and what a learner sees first is what sticks [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. You are the model: every briefing, checklist and sterile climb you fly becomes your learner's habit.

prereading.what: The 5P check, information, task and automation management, resources and workload, teaching decisions with scenarios, and grading SRM.
prereading.label: AIH 1-16 to 1-28

prereading.what: Positive exchange of flight controls, the sterile flight deck rule, using distractions, and not teaching at the wrong time.
prereading.label: AIH 9-8 to 9-10, 10-8

prereading.what: Checklist discipline, exchange of controls, ramp safety for passengers, baggage loading, and clearing the propeller area.
prereading.label: AFH 1-15 to 2-16

prereading.what: Resources, distractions, workload, the SAFETY briefing, sterile periods, autopilot planning, and automation management.
prereading.label: PHAK 2-23 to 2-31

prereading.what: Levels of automation, Anticipate-Act-Verify, armed and engaged modes, and training with automation.
prereading.label: RMH 7-1 to 7-4

prereading.what: What an EFB is, when it can replace paper, in-flight use, and what to assess and train.
prereading.label: AC 91-78A 7 to 11

prereading.what: Who decides PED use, the PED procedures an operator should set, passenger communication, and airborne cell phones.
prereading.label: AC 91.21-1D 7 to 9

warmup: Think first: your learner, a new private pilot, wants one dual flight with her two teenagers in the back seat before she flies them alone. She asks you to give the passenger briefing "because you do it better." Do you? What would you have her do instead, and what are you watching for from the right seat between the ramp and cruise?

key_terms.def: Before takeoff the PIC makes sure each person knows how to fasten and unfasten the belt and harness; before taxi, takeoff and landing each person is told to fasten them.
No nonessential talk or activity during critical phases of flight. A Part 121 rule (121.542) that the AIH says holds true for all pilots.
As defined in 121.542: all taxi, takeoff and landing ground operations, and all other flight below 10,000 feet except cruise.
Actions done from memory to configure the airplane, followed by a checklist that confirms the most critical items.
Reading a checklist item out loud and touching the control or switch, which makes it more likely the item was really done.
Practice past proficiency. It can make a checklist so automatic that the words come out without the thought or action behind them.
An engaged autopilot mode is controlling the airplane now; an armed mode will engage later, when its condition is met.
An electronic display, portable or installed, that shows paper-type information such as charts and the POH, or computes weight and balance or performance.
For Part 91 flights the person who decides which portable electronic devices may be used: the PIC or renter-pilot.
Flying a small non-turbine airplane without an MEL with an inoperative item that is not required, after it is removed or deactivated, placarded, and judged not a hazard.
A scheduled review of the Plan, the Plane, the Pilot, the Passengers and the Programming at set decision points before and during a flight.
Instructor tells and does, learner tells and instructor does, learner tells and does, then learner does and instructor evaluates.

body.p: Flight deck management is the set of habits that turn a pile of rules into a calm flight: who is in charge, what the passengers know, where things are stowed, what the avionics are doing and what the pilot will do next. Experienced pilots stress ground operations because hasty work there diminishes the margin of safety [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

Your job is to build habits, not just pass on facts. Establishing good habit patterns is a major objective of primary training, and the instructor should promote a positive attitude toward checklists [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. By the principle of primacy, the first way a learner does something tends to stick, so make sure it is right the first time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

head: What the ACS says
What it means for you
rows: Checklist use is evaluated throughout the practical test, with CRM, divided attention and visual scanning (ACS Appendix 2)
Every Task you teach is also a checklist and SRM lesson.
If an applicant fails to use ADM, including SRM/CRM, on any Task, that Task fails and this Task's ADM skill element goes on the notice of disapproval (ACS Appendix 2)
S4 of this Task is graded on the whole test, not only in the preflight.
The sterile flight deck should be taught and also modeled by the instructor [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Your own behavior in the climb is part of the lesson.

callout.text: Teach flight deck management on lesson one, before the learner has any bad habits to unlearn, and keep grading it on every flight after that.

check.q: Why does the principle of primacy matter so much for flight deck habits?
check.a: The first experience creates a strong impression, so the instructor must make sure the learner gets it right the first time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

body.p: The PIC is directly responsible for, and is the final authority on, the operation of the aircraft [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]]. Section 91.107 then sets three separate duties. Learners often merge them, so teach them apart.

head: Duty
When
Rule
rows: Brief how to fasten and unfasten the belt and, if installed, the shoulder harness
Before takeoff
Notify each person to fasten the belt and harness
Before moving on the surface, takeoff or landing
Each person in an approved seat with belt and harness secured
Movement on the surface, takeoff and landing
Required crewmembers belted at their stations; shoulder harness for takeoff and landing
Takeoff, landing and en route

body.p: Child rules: a child who has not reached the second birthday may be held by an adult in an approved seat [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]]. A child restraint system must carry the required labels, be secured to an approved forward-facing seat, and the child must be within its weight limit [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]]. Booster seats and vest- or harness-type restraints are not approved for aircraft unless they carry the FAA approval the rule describes [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)(B)(4)]].

Equipment rules back up the briefing. Day VFR requires an approved safety belt for each occupant 2 years of age or older [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(13)]]. Small airplanes made after July 18, 1978 need a shoulder harness for each front seat, and those made after December 12, 1986 need one for all seats [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(14)]].

Operation of the restraints starts on the preflight: belts and harnesses free from fraying, latching properly and securely attached; seats latched into the seat rails through the lock pins, with rail holes not worn oval [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

callout.text: Unless otherwise stated, 91.107 does not apply to Part 121, 125 or 135 operations, which have their own rules [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(b)]].

check.q: Your learner says, "I briefed the belts before engine start, so I'm done with 91.107." What is she missing?
check.a: The notification before moving on the surface, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]], and making sure everyone stays belted for those phases [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]].

chunks.title: The S2 briefing, item by item

body.p: The ACS lists what the briefing must include: the PIC, safety belts, shoulder harnesses, doors, passenger conduct, sterile aircraft, propeller blade avoidance and emergency procedures (ACS AI.V.B.S2). The PHAK SAFETY list covers most of it [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]], but not the PIC or the propeller, so a learner who only memorizes SAFETY will miss two items.

head: ACS item
What to brief
Source
rows: PIC
Who the PIC is, and on a dual flight the positive exchange of flight controls. If no one is designated PIC, several confident pilots' decision styles may conflict
Safety belts
How to fasten and unfasten; fastened for taxi, takeoff and landing; seat adjusted and locked
Shoulder harnesses
Fastened for takeoff and landing
Doors
How to secure and how to open. If a door opens in flight, nobody unbuckles to reach it; the pilot keeps flying and lands normally
Passenger conduct
No interfering with a crewmember; move on the ramp only as directed or with an escort; device rules
Sterile aircraft
No talking to the pilot from departure until clear of the local airspace, and from the first vector or descent for the approach
Propeller blade avoidance
Stay clear of the propeller; the pilot clears the area, calls "CLEAR" and waits for a response before starting
Emergency procedures
Fire extinguisher, exits, evacuation plan, survival kit, and what passengers do if something goes wrong

body.p: Add the rest of the PHAK list when it fits: smoking, route and altitudes, time en route, weather, the controls and what they do, and the airplane's capabilities and limits [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. AC 61-98E says the briefing should also give the pilot's procedures for minimizing cockpit distractions [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.1]].

callout.text: SAFETY plus P and P: the SAFETY list, then the PIC and the Propeller.

check.q: Which two ACS S2 items does the PHAK SAFETY list not cover?
check.a: Identifying the PIC and propeller blade avoidance. SAFETY covers belts, harness, doors, emergency items, traffic, talking and questions [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

body.p: The passenger briefing is a procedure, so teach it with the demonstration-performance method: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, then evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. In flight training this becomes the telling-and-doing technique.

head: Step
Applied to the briefing
rows: Instructor tells, instructor does
On lesson one you brief the learner exactly as you want it done, in the same order you will teach it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner tells you what goes in the briefing while you give it to a passenger or to an empty seat. Misunderstandings surface before the learner is busy [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Learner tells, learner does
The learner briefs you, thinking out loud [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Learner does, instructor evaluates
Learner self-assessment first, then yours, compared in discussion [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

body.p: Every dual briefing also includes the exchange of flight controls. Prior to any flight, brief the three-step process: "You have the flight controls," "I have the flight controls," "You have the flight controls," with a visual check [[24:37|AFH 1-16]].

Then build realism with scenarios: add a passenger who is nervous, a child, or a pilot friend who wants to help. Scenarios should start simple and grow in complexity as the learner can handle the workload [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

callout.text: Have the learner brief you as a real passenger on every flight, and ask one question a passenger would ask. Teach them to end with "What questions do you have?" [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]

check.q: Why put the "learner tells, instructor does" step in before the learner gives the briefing alone?
check.a: Freed from performing, the learner organizes the steps, and you can check understanding and correct a misunderstanding before habits form [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

body.p: A checklist is a memory aid that keeps critical items from being forgotten. It need not be a "do list": you can do the actions, then use the checklist to confirm, with the emphasis on the "check" in checklist. Checklists are of no value if the pilot is not committed to using them [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

bullets: At a minimum use prepared checklists for preflight, before engine start, engine starting, before taxi, before takeoff, after takeoff, cruise, descent, before landing, after landing, and shutdown and securing [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].
Flow, then check: a flow from memory configures the airplane, and a checklist of the most critical items confirms it [[59:17|AC 120-71B 5.1.2]].

Single pilot: read it out loud and touch each critical control [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]]. Mount the before-takeoff and before-landing checklists on the panel and use touch verification [[59:19|AC 120-71B 5.2.1]].
Anchor each checklist to a clear event; "floating" starts get rushed or forgotten [[59:18|AC 120-71B 5.1.5]].
Do the after-landing checklist only after stopping beyond the hold position markings, unless the manufacturer says otherwise [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].
If interrupted, restart from the beginning; slow down and confirm significant items [[59:22|AC 120-71B 5.6.4]].

body.p: The teaching problem is overlearning. A verbal checklist can become so automatic that the words are recited without the thoughts and actions they should trigger [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. Learners reluctant to use checklists can be reminded that pilots at all levels use them, and that the more advanced the airplane, the more crucial they are [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

On the checkride, when reading a checklist during a maneuver is unsafe or impractical, the evaluator assesses the memory items and the review of the checklist once conditions permit (ACS Appendix 2). Teach learners the same pattern for emergencies: memory items first, checklist after.

callout.text: Fast, perfect recitation is not proof of a good checklist. Watch the learner's eyes and hands, not just the words.

check.q: Your learner reads the before-takeoff checklist flawlessly in eight seconds, eyes on the card. What is the AIH name for this risk?
check.a: Overlearning: the recitation has become decoupled from the thoughts and actions the items should trigger [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

body.p: Databases drive the GPS, the moving map and the EFB, and they go out of date. Databases are updated every 28 days [[23:30|IFH 1-11]]. The 5P check counts database currency as part of the Plane [[25:21|AIH 1-17]], and the PIC must become familiar with all available information concerning the flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

head: Use
Requirement
rows: IFR

Databases must be updated for IFR operations [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. Onboard data must be current and appropriate for the region, with the navaids, waypoints and terminal procedures for the departure, arrival and alternate airports [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].
Approaches
Every approach flown must be retrievable by name from the current database; manual entry of approach waypoints is not permitted [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].
VFR

Databases should be updated but there is no requirement. Do not use a moving map with an outdated database in and around critical airspace; verify waypoints with current products such as the Chart Supplement or a sectional [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].
EFB
Data used for navigation or performance planning must be current, up to date and valid, as verified by the pilot [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]].
Paper backup
The moving map is never a substitute for a VFR sectional or low altitude en route chart [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

body.p: Verification steps. Preflight: find the issue date, confirm the date and time of use are before the expiration, and check that the provider has not published a notice limiting a waypoint or procedure [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. In flight: waypoint names must match the chart, and the waypoints must be logical in location and order [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]].

Why it matters: numerous pilots have flown into airspace they were trying to avoid by using an outdated database. Without a current database, disregard the moving map for critical navigation decisions [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]].

callout.text: Make "show me the expiration date" a standing preflight question, for the panel GPS and the learner's own tablet. Let them find it themselves.

check.q: Your learner's tablet database expired last week. You are flying VFR near a Class B shelf. What does the AIM recommend?
check.a: No update is required for VFR, but do not rely on the outdated moving map in and around critical airspace; verify waypoints with current products such as the sectional or Chart Supplement [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

body.p: Supervise baggage loading yourself. Unsecured or badly loaded baggage can change the center of gravity [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. If a 30-lb bag slides aft in flight, the CG moves by weight shifted times distance shifted divided by total weight [[22:24|W&B Handbook 2-4]].

Part 91 has no general cargo rule for small airplanes. The cargo rule for large and turbine multiengine airplanes [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501(a)]] gives a clear standard to teach. Unless it is in an approved rack, bin or compartment, cargo must be [[60:535|14 CFR 91.525(a)]] [[60:536|14 CFR 91.525(a)(3)]]:

bullets: Tied down by a belt or tiedown strong enough that it cannot shift in all normal flight and ground conditions.
Packaged or covered so it cannot injure passengers.
Within the load limits of the seats and floor.
Clear of every required emergency or regular exit and the aisle.
Not carried directly above seated passengers.

head: Item
How to secure it
rows: Maps, charts and loose items
Remove and stow objects on the glare shield in flight [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]; organize cockpit materials before flight to leave more time to scan [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Tablet or EFB
Plan its mounting and stowage for takeoff and landing; an unsecured EFB is its own hazard [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]].
Passenger devices
Tell passengers how and when PEDs must be secured or stowed [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 8.1]].
Seats and belts
Seats latched into the seat rails and belts free from fraying and securely attached [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
Airplane after flight
Control locks and security locks installed; tied down or hangared [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

callout.text: Teach a cabin sweep just before engine start: the learner points at and touches each loose item and says where it is secured. Weight limits and tie-down points come from the POH/AFM.

check.q: A passenger sets a soft cooler on the empty seat beside her with no belt around it. Which items of the 91.525 standard does it fail?
check.a: It is not tied down so it could shift, and it may not be packaged to prevent injury; you also check seat load limits and exits [[60:536|14 CFR 91.525(a)(3)]].

body.p: Used well, automation reduces workload and frees attention for the flight path [[30:50|RMH 7-1]]. It can also create more work and confusion, lull pilots into complacency, and erode manual skill [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. Humans are poor passive monitors, and the more reliable the system the worse they monitor [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

head: Teach this
Why
rows: When to use it and when not to
One of the most important ideas of automation management; the learner must also fly without it [[25:23|AIH 1-19]].
Know engaged and armed modes
At the most basic level, know which modes are engaged and which are armed, and verify armed modes engage on time [[25:23|AIH 1-19]].
Callouts
Practice callouts, especially after arming a course or altitude change [[25:23|AIH 1-19]].
Anticipate, Act, Verify
Know what should happen, push the button, confirm it happened [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
Step down a level
One of the most common errors is failing to move to a lower level of automation when things change [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
Stop, look and read
Read the display before pushing, pulling or twisting anything [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]].
Program on the ground
Check all programming before departure against a paper log; if the two differ, do not assume the computer is right [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

body.p: Plan when to program. Avionics tend to capture attention for long periods, so decide in advance when and where to program approaches and route changes, and when not to [[25:22|AIH 1-18]]. Train automation under VFR with a qualified instructor before IFR, and use a flight simulation training device to repeat procedures under high workload [[30:52|RMH 7-3]] [[30:53|RMH 7-4]].
Grade it progressively. In the AIH example, automation management is a "describe" item on flight one, a "practice" item by flight three and a "manage-decide" item by flight five [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

callout.text: Before teaching in an unfamiliar avionics suite, familiarize yourself, from the manuals to flight time if needed. Unfamiliarity creates a hazard [[25:190|AIH 10-6]] [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: On a practice approach the learner arms the approach mode and says nothing. On the annunciator, LOC and GS are white. What should she have said, and what do the white labels mean?
check.a: A callout of the armed modes [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]. White LOC and GS mean approach mode is armed but not engaged [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

body.p: An EFB is an electronic display, portable or installed, that shows paper-type information such as checklists, charts and the POH, or computes things like weight and balance and performance [[42:2|AC 91-78A 7.1]]. A tablet is a PED, so its use must meet 91.21 and be evaluated first so it will not interfere with the airplane [[42:2|AC 91-78A 7.2]].

Under Part 91 an EFB may replace paper in all phases of flight when it replaces no required navigation, communication or surveillance equipment, shows only information equivalent to the paper, uses data that is current and verified by the pilot, and meets 91.21 [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]. In-flight use is the decision of the operator and the PIC [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.2]].

bullets: Assess workload, flight deck integration, display and lighting, shutdown and failures, and stowage; inputs get harder in flight [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]].
Train preflight checks, every function, when not to use it, and cross-checking entries and results [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.2]].
If the applicant uses an EFB on the practical test, expect to show knowledge, risk management and skill with it (ACS Appendix 3).

head: PED question
Answer
rows: Where does 91.21 apply?
Aircraft of air carrier or operating certificate holders, and any other aircraft under IFR [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(a)]].
What is always allowed?
Portable voice recorders, hearing aids, heart pacemakers and electric shavers [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(b)]].
Who decides on other devices?
For aircraft other than certificate holders, the PIC or other operator [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(c)]]. The AC calls the PIC or renter-pilot the operator [[43:2|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]].
Airplane not shown PED tolerant?
The operator may allow PEDs during cruise; a device causing interference should be turned off [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]].
Cell phones?
The FCC prohibits airborne cellular use. Passengers turn phones off, disable cellular transmit, or use airplane mode [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.1-9.2]].

body.p: Teach learners to write a short PED policy for their own flights: which devices, when, how they are stowed, which modes, how passengers are told, and what to do about interference or battery smoke or fire [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 8.1]].

callout.text: Application: once in a while, ask the learner what they would do if the tablet went dark right now. The answer should not depend on the tablet.

check.q: On an IFR training flight, may your learner's passenger use a laptop?
check.a: Only if the PIC or other operator has determined it will not interfere with the navigation or communication systems [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(b)(5),(c)]].

body.p: First teach the legal path. Without an MEL, a small non-turbine airplane may fly with an inoperative item if it is not part of the VFR-day type certification equipment, not required by the equipment list or KOEL for the operation, not required by 91.205 or another rule, and not required by an AD; it is removed or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative"; and a rated pilot or mechanic determines it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

Deactivation may take more than a switch, such as pulling and securing a breaker. It is not preventive maintenance, and a person authorized under 43.7 must make the maintenance record entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. The placard is legible and next to the control without hiding others [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]].
Then teach that legal is only the start. Before flying with an inoperative item, weigh [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]:

bullets: Departure, destination and en route environment
Extra workload, fatigue and other human factors

body.p: The PHAK example: a dead autopilot can be the single factor that takes a night approach into an unfamiliar airport from medium to serious risk, so decide before departure how a failure would be handled [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

Instructor angle. Training airplanes are often not under your control, so you may not know about inoperative systems or overdue inspections [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Determine the official airworthiness status before the flight, review the discrepancy report, resolve questions with maintenance, and involve the learner [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. When a discrepancy turns up on a preflight, let the learner decide first, then discuss the options [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

callout.text: On the checkride, inoperative equipment must not interfere with the practical test requirements (ACS Appendix 3).

check.q: The school's airplane has a placarded inoperative autopilot and the 91.213(d) steps are done. Your learner says, "It's legal, so we're good." What do you teach?
check.a: Legal is not the whole answer: weigh workload, weather, night, airports and diversions with the item inoperative [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]], as the PHAK autopilot example shows [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

chunks.title: Passenger distractions and the sterile flight deck

body.p: A contributing factor in many accidents is a distraction that pulls attention from the instruments or the outside view. Many start small and end badly because the pilot stops controlling the airplane [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Most stall and spin accidents happened when attention was diverted from flying [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

The sterile flight deck rule (121.542) bars airline crews from nonessential activities during critical phases: taxi, takeoff and landing, and all flight below 10,000 feet except cruise. The AIH says the idea holds for the whole aviation community and that the instructor should teach and model it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. For general aviation, the PHAK sets sterile periods from departure to the first intermediate altitude and clear of the local airspace, and from the first vector or descent for the approach [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. AC 61-98E adds taxi [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.5]].

head: Distraction
Teach the learner to
rows: Chatty passenger in the climb
Brief the sterile periods before engine start and keep passengers informed when workload is low [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Any passenger, even an examiner
Tell them when their actions distract from safe flight; the PIC must know when to say so [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].
Interference or intoxication
No one may interfere with a crewmember [[60:436|14 CFR 91.11]]; except in an emergency, do not carry a person who appears intoxicated [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]].
Door pops open
Fly the airplane, do not unbuckle, do not rush to land; open-door accidents come from distraction [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Passenger schedule pressure
Involve passengers in the decision with a factual description of the risks, and plan an out such as a rental car [[25:21|AIH 1-17]] [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].

body.p: Passengers can also help. They can watch for traffic, read checklist items, and notice a strange smell or sound [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]]. Brief them so they are comfortable voicing concerns [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

Do not be the distraction. Avoid teaching at an inappropriate time, such as discussing takeoff technique while entering the runway [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Do most takeoff teaching before contacting the tower or announcing on the CTAF [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

callout.text: Use planned distractions to train, like asking for something from the back seat or a heading to an airport [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], but only at a safe altitude and never in the sterile periods you are teaching.

check.q: Where do the PHAK's general aviation sterile periods differ from the 121.542 definition the AIH quotes?
check.a: The PHAK ties them to departure until the first intermediate altitude and clear of local airspace, and arrival from the first vector or descent [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; 121.542 covers taxi, takeoff, landing and all flight below 10,000 feet except cruise [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

body.p: SRM is managing all resources, on board and outside, available to a single pilot [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]. The AFH lists it as situational awareness, human resource management, task management and ADM [[24:50|AFH 2-13]]. A practical tool is the 5P check: the Plan, the Plane, the Pilot, the Passengers and the Programming [[25:20|AIH 1-16]].

head: P
Flight deck management content
rows: Plan
Weather, route, fuel, publications currency; updated through the flight [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].
Plane
Mechanical issues plus database currency, automation status and backup systems [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].
Pilot
Fatigue and late-flight complacency, which peak just as the hardest part of the flight arrives [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].
Passengers
Sit within arm's reach and bring schedule pressure; involve them in decisions [[25:21|AIH 1-17]] [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].
Programming
Plan when and where to program, and when not to [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].

body.p: Run it at preflight, before takeoff, hourly or at the midpoint, before descent, and before the final approach fix or, VFR, before entering the pattern [[25:20|AIH 1-16]]. On flights longer than 2 hours, do it hourly [[25:21|AIH 1-17]]. When weighing options, being on time, inconveniencing passengers or people waiting, and reaching the original destination come after safety [[30:55|RMH 8-2]].

Teaching it. Turn planning and decisions over to the learner as soon as possible and become a mentor [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]. Assess how decisions were made, not only whether maneuvers were accurate [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Grade SRM as Explain, Practice, Manage/Decide or Not Observed [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. With an instructor aboard, CRM applies: brief roles, and use the positive exchange of controls (ACS Appendix 2).

callout.text: 5 Ps, 5 times: preflight, pretakeoff, midpoint (hourly if over 2 hours), predescent, pre-FAF or pattern entry.

check.q: At what points does the AIH say to run the 5P check?
check.a: Preflight, before takeoff, hourly or at the midpoint, before descent, and before the final approach fix or, VFR, before entering the pattern [[25:20|AIH 1-16]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: a flight deck management lesson

head: Phase
What you do
rows: Ground: explanation
Give the objective and completion standard, cover safety, and invite questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Brief the exchange of controls [[24:37|AFH 1-16]].
Ramp: escort and load
Move passengers only as directed; supervise baggage loading; learner does the cabin sweep [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].
Before start: brief
Learner gives the S2 briefing to you or a real passenger (ACS AI.V.B.S2). Application: step in before start only for missing safety items; save the rest for the debrief.
Before taxi: program
Set up radios and navigation before taxi; setup on the roll is a leading cause of heads-down taxi [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.3]]. Verify programming against the plan [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].
Taxi to climb: sterile
You model silence except for flight duties; teaching happens before contacting the tower [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Cruise: workload
Gradually increase workload and watch how the learner manages it; when overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].
Debrief
Learner self-assessment, then yours, then compare [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

body.p: Delegation is a skill to teach. When overloaded, a pilot can hand a task to another pilot or passenger, use the autopilot, or ask ATC for help [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]. Prepare for high workload during low workload: review charts and set frequencies early, and do checklists well in advance [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

callout.text: The S elements have no number tolerance. The examiner judges whether you demonstrate and explain at the same time, so practice narrating the briefing, the cabin sweep and the automation setup out loud.

check.q: Where should most of your teaching about a takeoff happen, and why?
check.a: Before contacting the tower or announcing on the CTAF, so you avoid over-stimulating the learner and keep a sterile flight deck [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Briefing from SAFETY only
No mention of the PIC or the propeller
Add the two ACS items; brief the PIC and the start procedure [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] (ACS AI.V.B.S2)
Brief but no notify
Belts briefed at the ramp, no call before taxi or landing
Teach the three separate 91.107 duties [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)]]
Checklist recited, not checked
Fast recitation, eyes not on the items [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]
Slow down, read deliberately, touch each critical item [[59:22|AC 120-71B 5.6.4]] [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]]
Lost place after an interruption
Guesses where it left off
Restart that section from the beginning [[59:22|AC 120-71B 5.6.2]]
Database never checked
Cannot say when the data expires
Make it a preflight item; IFR must be current [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]
Loose items
Tablet on the seat, chart on the glare shield
Mount or stow; cabin sweep before start [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]] [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]]
Mode confusion
Surprised when a mode does not capture
Callouts after each change; Anticipate, Act, Verify [[25:23|AIH 1-19]] [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]
Head-down reprogramming
Path wanders while typing a change
Step down a level or hand fly, then reprogram [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]
Talking passengers in the climb
Learner answers questions and drifts off altitude or heading
Brief sterile periods and enforce them politely [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]
Legal means safe
Flies with an inoperative item without a risk look
Run the AC 91-67A analysis [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]

callout.text: When a learner errs, ask why it happened and what would prevent it, but do not let them practice the wrong thing [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

check.q: Your learner drifts 200 feet off altitude while reprogramming a reroute with the autopilot in NAV. What do you teach?
check.a: Reduce the level of automation or fly manually, keep the flight path under control, then reprogram [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

f1.caption: Figure 1-9. The 5P checklist. (AIH 1-16)
f1.alt: Five overlapping colored circles around a green star labeled 5P Check List: Plan at the top in teal, Plane at right in green, Passengers at lower right in orange, Programming at lower left in blue, and Pilot at left in purple.

f2.caption: Figure 2-17. When possible, have a passenger reconfirm that critical tasks are completed. (PHAK 2-23)
f2.alt: View from behind a pilot in a light twin on final approach to a runway near a coastline, with an inset yellow Before Landing Check card listing items such as fuel shut-off valve, radios, altimeter, seat belts and harnesses and boost pumps, beside a picture of a landing gear leg and wheel.

f3.caption: Figure 9-7. This comparison of steps in the teaching process, the demonstration-performance method, and the telling-and-doing technique highlights similarities as well as differences. The main difference in the telling-and-doing technique is the important transition, learner tells, instructor does, which occurs between the second and third step. (AIH 9-7)
f3.alt: A three-column table. Traditional Teaching Process: Preparation, Presentation, Application, Review and Evaluation. Demonstration-Performance Method: Explanation, Demonstration, Learner performance supervision, Evaluation. Telling-and-Doing Technique: Preparation; Instructor tells, Instructor does; a highlighted Learner tells, Instructor does; Learner tells, Learner does; Learner does, Instructor evaluates.

f4.caption: Figure 7-3. Flight mode annunciators in green indicate the autopilot is engaged in heading "HDG" and altitude "ALT" mode, maintaining 9,000 feet MSL. The white "LOC" and "GS" annunciators indicate approach mode is armed but not engaged. (RMH 7-3)
f4.alt: Black annunciator strip reading LOC (white), HDG (green), AP (green), ALT (green), 9000FT (green), GS (white).

f5.caption: Figure 9-8. During this procedure, a visual check is recommended to see that the other person actually has the flight controls. There should never be any doubt about who is flying the aircraft. (AIH 9-9)
f5.alt: Three stacked steps titled Positive Exchange of Flight Controls: the instructor says you have the flight controls, the learner answers I have the flight controls, and the instructor again says you have the flight controls.

f6.caption: Figure 1-14. Accidents often occur when flying task requirements exceed pilot capabilities. The difference between these two factors is called the margin of safety; in this idealized example it is minimal during the approach and landing. (AIH 1-26)
f6.alt: A 3D ribbon chart of task load over time through preflight, takeoff, cruise and approach and landing. A Pilot Capabilities band and a Task Requirements band rise and fall; the orange Margin of Safety between them shrinks almost to nothing at approach and landing.

scenario.title: A checkout flight with the family aboard
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. A recently certificated private pilot books a VFR dual flight in the school's glass-cockpit trainer with her two teenagers in the back seat, so you can watch her fly them before she does it alone. The squawk sheet shows the autopilot placarded INOP. She brings her own tablet as an EFB, a backpack and a soft cooler. The kids plan to film the flight on their phones. Her briefing is quick: belts, doors and the fire extinguisher. In the climb one teenager asks a question and she turns around to answer.

questions.q: Before the lesson, what do you check about the airplane, and how do you involve her?
questions.a: Determine its official airworthiness status and review the discrepancy report, resolving any question with maintenance before the preflight, and involve the learner [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. For the autopilot, check that the 91.213(d) conditions are met [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

questions.q: With you and a rated pilot both aboard, how do you settle who is PIC and who is flying?
questions.a: Agree on and brief who is PIC; with several confident pilots and no designated PIC, decision styles can conflict [[25:21|AIH 1-17]]. Brief the three-step exchange of flight controls before flight [[24:37|AFH 1-16]].

questions.q: Her briefing missed several S2 items. When and how do you fix it?
questions.a: Let it run, then debrief with her self-assessment first and your assessment after [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. She still needs the PIC, harnesses, conduct, sterile periods, the propeller and emergency procedures (ACS AI.V.B.S2) [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

questions.q: Can the teenagers film with their phones on this VFR flight?
questions.a: 91.21 applies to certificate holders and IFR flight [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(a)]], but airborne cellular use is prohibited by the FCC, so phones go to airplane mode [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.1-9.2]]. Brief when devices are stowed [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 8.1]].

questions.q: Where do the backpack and cooler go?
questions.a: In the baggage area within POH limits, loaded under the pilot's supervision [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Anything in the cabin is tied down so it cannot shift and does not block an exit [[60:536|14 CFR 91.525(a)(3)]].

questions.q: She turns to answer a question in the climb. What do you do and teach?
questions.a: Keep the airplane safe first, then teach the sterile period from departure until clear of the local airspace and how to tell passengers to hold questions [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. The PIC must know when to tell any passenger that they are distracting [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

skills.do: Secure all items in the aircraft. There is no numeric tolerance. Expect to demonstrate a cabin sweep while explaining it as you would to a learner: baggage loaded and tied down so it cannot shift or block an exit, glare shield clear, EFB mounted or stowed, and to explain how you teach and check it.
skills.practice: Before every flight, do a cabin sweep out loud against the 91.525 standard [[60:536|14 CFR 91.525(a)(3)]] and the glare shield rule [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Teach it to a friend using telling-and-doing [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

skills.do: Conduct an appropriate passenger briefing, including identifying the PIC, use of safety belts, shoulder harnesses, doors, passenger conduct, sterile aircraft, propeller blade avoidance, and emergency procedures (ACS AI.V.B.S2). No numeric tolerance: give it as a model for a learner and explain why each item is there.
skills.practice: Write a briefing card from the SAFETY list plus the PIC and propeller [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], and give it to a real passenger until it is natural and short. Add the exchange of controls for dual flights [[24:37|AFH 1-16]].

skills.do: Properly program and manage the aircraft's automation, as applicable (ACS AI.V.B.S3). No numeric tolerance: program before taxi, verify it, call engaged and armed modes, step down a level on a change, disconnect and hand fly, and explain each step as a lesson.
skills.practice: Practice with the avionics simulator or a flight simulation training device under high workload [[30:53|RMH 7-4]], and fly Anticipate, Act, Verify with callouts on every change [[30:51|RMH 7-2]] [[25:23|AIH 1-19]].

skills.do: Appropriately manage risks by utilizing ADM, including SRM/CRM (ACS AI.V.B.S4). No numeric tolerance; the examiner watches this on every Task, and a failure to use ADM fails that Task (ACS Appendix 2). Talk through threats, use the 5P check, and show how you teach and grade SRM.
skills.practice: Run the 5P check at each decision point on your own flights [[25:20|AIH 1-16]]. Build one scenario for a learner with a destination, outcome, performance level and planned changes [[25:31|AIH 1-27]], and practice grading it [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

quiz.q: A small airplane was manufactured in 1990. Under 14 CFR 91.205, which seats need a shoulder harness or restraint system?
options: Only the pilot's seat
Only the front seats
All seats
None; harnesses are optional
quiz.why: Small airplanes manufactured after December 12, 1986 need an approved shoulder harness or restraint system for all seats [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(14)]].

quiz.q: Which ACS S2 briefing item is NOT part of the PHAK SAFETY list?
options: Fire extinguisher location
Exit doors
Propeller blade avoidance
Traffic scanning
quiz.why: SAFETY covers seat belts, air vents, fire extinguisher, exits, traffic, talking and questions [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; propeller blade avoidance comes from the ACS and the AFH start procedure [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

quiz.q: In the telling-and-doing technique, which step is the learner's only passive one?
options: Instructor tells, instructor does
Learner tells, instructor does
Learner tells, learner does
Learner does, instructor evaluates
quiz.why: The instructor's demonstration with explanation is the only step in which the learner plays a passive role [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

quiz.q: Your learner's checklist has become a fast recitation that no longer triggers any action. What does the AIH call the cause?
options: Primacy
Overlearning
Transfer of learning
Habit interference
quiz.why: Overlearning can make a verbal checklist so automatic that the recitation is decoupled from the thoughts and actions it should trigger [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

quiz.q: During flight, what does the AIM say to check on a procedure retrieved from the database?
options: The latitude and longitude of every waypoint
That waypoint names match the chart and the waypoints are logical in location and order
Only the final approach fix altitude
Nothing; the preflight check is enough
quiz.why: In flight, check that names match the chart and the waypoints are logical; there is no specific requirement to check each latitude and longitude [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]].

quiz.q: The AIM tells pilots to remove and stow maps on the glare shield in flight. Under which topic?
options: Cockpit lighting
Visual obstructions in the cockpit, under collision avoidance
Magnetic compass errors
Fire prevention
quiz.why: It is listed under visual obstructions in the cockpit in Judgment Aspects of Collision Avoidance [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

quiz.q: In the AIH's progressive SRM grading example, at what level should automation management be graded by flight five?
options: Describe
Explain
Practice
Manage-decide
quiz.why: Describe on flight one, practice by flight three, manage-decide by flight five [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

quiz.q: Under AC 91.21-1D, if an operator has not shown its airplane to be PED tolerant, when may it allow PED use?
options: Never
During cruise flight
Only on the ground
During all phases if in airplane mode
quiz.why: If PED tolerance has not been demonstrated, the operator may allow PED operation during cruise flight [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]].

quiz.q: You will teach in a flying club's airplane you do not maintain. What does the AIH say to do before the flight?
options: Trust the club's scheduling system
Determine the official airworthiness status and review the current discrepancy report
Only check the fuel
Ask the last renter how it flew
quiz.why: Determine the official airworthiness status before scheduled flights, know the operator's procedures for discrepancies, and review the current discrepancy report [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

quiz.q: When does the AIH say to do most of the teaching for a takeoff lesson?
options: During the takeoff roll
Right after liftoff
Before contacting the tower or announcing on the CTAF
In the debrief only
quiz.why: Do the majority of the teaching before contacting the tower or announcing on the CTAF, which helps maintain a sterile flight deck [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: A passenger brings a car booster seat for her 6-year-old and asks to use it in the back seat. What does 91.107 say?
options: It is fine if it is belted in
Booster-type restraints are not approved for aircraft unless they carry the FAA approval the rule describes
Any child seat sold in the U.S. is approved
It is allowed only for children under 2
final_quiz.why: Booster-type, vest-type and harness-type child restraints are not approved for use in aircraft except as provided in the labeling rules [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)(B)(4)]].

final_quiz.q: At the ramp, your learner's friend smells of alcohol and is slurring words. Your learner is PIC. What applies?
options: He may ride if he sits in the back
Except in an emergency, a person who appears intoxicated may not be carried
Only the pilot is limited by alcohol rules
He may ride if he promises not to talk
final_quiz.why: Except in an emergency, no pilot may allow a person who appears to be intoxicated to be carried [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]].

final_quiz.q: On your CFI checkride the examiner, playing a passenger, starts a long conversation as you climb into busy airspace. What do the sources support?
options: Keep talking; the examiner is in charge
Politely tell the examiner the conversation must wait until workload drops
Ignore the examiner without saying anything
Hand the controls to the examiner
final_quiz.why: A PIC must know when to tell any passenger, even a DPE, that their actions distract from the safe conduct of the flight [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner reads the before-takeoff checklist perfectly but never looks at or touches the fuel selector. What fix fits the sources best?
options: Have her memorize it instead
Have her read deliberately, slow down on significant items and touch each critical control
Skip the checklist for routine flights
Let her read faster to save time
final_quiz.why: Read the checklist deliberately and slow down to confirm significant items [[59:22|AC 120-71B 5.6.4]]; touching a control while reading it further confirms the item was done [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]].

final_quiz.q: Your instrument student's panel GPS database expired yesterday. Tomorrow's lesson is an IFR flight with an RNAV approach. What applies?
options: Fly it with the paper chart as backup
Databases must be updated for IFR; the approach must come from the current database
Expired data is fine for 7 days
Enter the approach waypoints manually
final_quiz.why: Databases must be updated for IFR operations [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]], and approaches must be retrieved by name from the current database, not entered manually [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants her tablet's POH app to replace the paper POH on Part 91 flights. Which is one of the AC 91-78A conditions?
options: The tablet must be FAA certified
It must show only information functionally equivalent to the paper it replaces
It needs a letter of authorization
It must be connected to aircraft power
final_quiz.why: An EFB may replace paper when, among other criteria, it displays only information functionally equivalent to the paper reference [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]], with no formal approval needed for Part 91 [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.2]].

final_quiz.q: On a practice approach the autopilot does not capture altitude as expected, and your learner starts pressing buttons while the airplane climbs. What does the RMH support?
options: Keep pressing until it works
Reduce the level of automation or fly manually, then take time to resolve it
Turn off the avionics master
Ask ATC to fix it
final_quiz.why: If the automation is not working as expected, the pilot may reduce the level of automation, fly manually and take time to resolve the condition [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: You arrive for a lesson and the squawk sheet says the attitude indicator is "intermittent," with no maintenance entry. What does the AIH say to do?
options: Fly; the learner needs practice with partial panel
Resolve the airworthiness question with maintenance before the preflight, and involve the learner
Placard it yourself and go
Let the learner decide alone and accept the choice
final_quiz.why: Any questions regarding airworthiness status should be resolved with maintenance personnel before conducting the preflight, and the instructor should consider involving the learner [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: An item is legally deferred under 91.213(d). Which question belongs in the AC 91-67A safety risk analysis before flying?
options: Whether the item is expensive
How the inoperative item interacts with other failures, weather, night and crew workload
Whether the last pilot complained
Whether the placard is in color
final_quiz.why: The analysis includes the interrelationship of multiple failures, adverse weather, night, airports, diversion options, workload, fatigue and human factors [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a 3.5-hour cross-country with a learner. How often does the AIH say to run the 5P check during the cruise portion?
options: Never in cruise
Once, at the midpoint
Hourly
Every 15 minutes
final_quiz.why: If the flight is longer than 2 hours, the 5P check should be conducted hourly [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

final_quiz.q: After a flight, your learner could name the risks of the planned route only after you prompted her. Using the AIH SRM grades, which grade fits?
options: Explain
Practice
Manage/Decide
Not Observed
final_quiz.why: Explain: the learner can verbally identify and describe the risks but needs to be prompted to identify risks and make decisions [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

final_quiz.q: You are designing a scenario to train flight deck management. Which feature does the AIH say a good scenario has?
options: It is a pass/fail test
It has one correct answer
It is interactive and requires time-pressured decisions
It should lead the learner into errors
final_quiz.why: A good scenario is not a test, has no single correct answer, is interactive, should not promote errors, and requires time-pressured decisions [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

final_quiz.q: On an IFR flight, a squeal appears in the headsets each time a passenger's laptop is opened. What does AC 91.21-1D say to do?
options: Turn up the volume
Turn off the device responsible for the interference
Switch radios and keep the laptop on
Report it after landing only
final_quiz.why: If interference is experienced, isolate the devices and turn off the one responsible [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]].

takeaways: You teach habits: model the briefing, the checklist and the sterile climb on every flight, and get it right the first time.
91.107 has three duties: brief before takeoff, notify before taxi, takeoff and landing, and keep everyone belted for those phases.
The S2 briefing is SAFETY plus the PIC and the propeller, taught with telling-and-doing.
Checklists need the check: read deliberately, touch critical items, anchor each list, restart after interruptions.
IFR data must be current; VFR data should be, and an outdated moving map is not trusted near critical airspace.
Automation: know engaged and armed modes, call them out, step down a level when things change, and grade it progressively.
Legal is not the same as safe for inoperative equipment, and passengers are both a resource and a distraction.
cfi_notes: Sources differ on the sterile period. The AIH quotes the 121.542 critical phases (taxi, takeoff, landing and all flight below 10,000 feet except cruise) [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]; the PHAK uses departure to the first intermediate altitude and clear of local airspace, and arrival from the first vector or descent [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; AC 61-98E adds taxi [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.5]]. None is a Part 91 rule. Teach learners to brief their own sterile periods, including taxi.

Handbook line to correct: PHAK 9-10 says deactivation may be as simple as pulling a circuit breaker [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. AC 91-67A says deactivation is not preventive maintenance and an authorized person under 43.7 must make the 43.9 record entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. Teach the AC.
PHAK 2-27 and 2-29 still say to fly to the standards of the PTS [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]] [[1:68|PHAK 2-29]]. The current standard is the ACS; say so when you use those pages.
The SAFETY list is a good start but does not cover two ACS S2 items, the PIC and propeller blade avoidance. Teach learners to add them, or they will miss them on their own checkrides.
91.525 cargo rules legally apply only to Part 91 subpart F airplanes [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501(a)]]. Use them as a teaching standard for small airplanes and say that clearly.
Your own unfamiliarity with an avionics suite is a hazard [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]; familiarize yourself before you teach in it [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
Let the learner make the first call on squawks, PED questions and passenger requests, then discuss. Decisions about typical issues build judgment [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].
Remind applicants of ACS Appendix 2: failing to use ADM on any Task fails that Task and lists this Task's ADM element on the disapproval, so S4 is graded all test long.
gaps: No source gives airplane-specific baggage limits, tie-down points, seat or floor load limits, or door and exit procedures; use the POH/AFM.
Autopilot mode logic, database expiration displays and EFB functions vary by manufacturer; the avionics pilot's guide or AFM supplement is needed.
No source gives one approved passenger briefing script for Part 91; the ACS list, 91.107 and the PHAK SAFETY list must be combined by the instructor.
The sources do not give a Part 91 rule for a sterile flight deck; it is guidance from the AIH, PHAK and AC 61-98E.
This Task's Skills elements have no numeric ACS tolerances.

activities.title: Match the rule to the duty
activities.intro: Tap a rule, then what it requires.

pairs.r: Brief each person on fastening and unfastening the belt before takeoff
Notify each person to fasten the belt before taxi, takeoff and landing
Required crewmembers stay at their stations with belts fastened
No one may interfere with a crewmember doing their duties
Do not carry a person who appears intoxicated, except in an emergency
An approved safety belt for each occupant 2 years of age or older

activities.title: True or false: navigation data
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: For VFR flight, the AIM requires a current GPS database.
cards.why: False. Databases should be updated, but there is no requirement for VFR navigation [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

cards.s: Navigation databases are updated every 28 days.
An approach may be flown from waypoints entered by latitude and longitude if the database lacks it.
cards.why: False. Manual entry of waypoints is not permitted for approach procedures [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

cards.s: Before using the database, the pilot should check that the provider has not published a notice limiting a waypoint or procedure.
cards.why: True. It is a preflight verification step [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

cards.s: Under AC 91-78A, the pilot verifies that EFB navigation and performance data is current and valid.
Without a current database, the PHAK says to disregard the moving map when making critical navigation decisions.

activities.title: Data and cargo numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your database cycle started 20 days ago. Databases are updated every 28 days. How many days until the next update?
You depart at 1400Z with an estimated time en route of 2 hours 40 minutes. The IFR database expires at 1601Z. For how many minutes of the planned flight would the data be expired?
items.why: Arrival 1400Z + 2:40 = 1640Z; 1640Z - 1601Z = 39 minutes. The time of use should be before the expiration [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

items.q: A 30-lb camera case slides aft 45 inches in a 2,400-lb airplane. How far does the CG move?
items.why: Change in CG = 30 x 45 / 2,400 = 1,350 / 2,400 = 0.5625 inches aft [[22:24|W&B Handbook 2-4]].

items.q: A 60-lb cooler has an 18-inch by 24-inch base. What floor load does it impose?
items.why: Area = 18 x 24 / 144 = 3 sq ft; 60 / 3 = 20 lb per sq ft [[22:81|W&B Handbook 9-9]].

activities.title: Devices on a Part 91 IFR flight
activities.intro: Tap a device, then where it belongs on an IFR flight in a privately operated airplane.
buckets: Only if the PIC determines no interference
Cellular transmit must be off once airborne

activities.title: Where does it go in the 5P check?
activities.intro: Drag each item to the P where the AIH puts it.

pins.label: Weather, route, fuel and publications currency
When and where to load approaches

activities.title: 5P decision points
activities.intro: Put the 5P decision points in the order they come in a VFR flight, then tap Check.
steps: Preflight, in the flight planning room
Midpoint of the flight, or hourly on long flights
Before descent into the terminal area
Just before entering the traffic pattern

activities.title: A passenger flight, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are giving a dual lesson to a private pilot who is flying her father, a non-pilot, for the first time. You sit right seat as the instructor.

steps.s: At the ramp, the fuel truck pulls up while her father is already seated in the back.
options: Leave him aboard to save time
Have passengers get out, and have the pilot witness the refueling
Let the line person handle it alone
Start the engine to stay warm
steps.why: During refueling it is advisable to remove all passengers and witness the refueling to make sure the right fuel and quantity go in and caps are secured [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

steps.s: Her briefing covers belts, doors and the extinguisher. She is about to start the engine.
options: Stop her now and redo it
Let her start; debrief the missing items after the flight
Brief the missing safety items yourself before start, then debrief her
Ignore it; it was close enough
steps.why: Propeller avoidance and the start procedure matter before start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], so cover the safety items now, then let her self-assess before you add your assessment [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

steps.s: On taxi she starts loading the GPS route while the airplane rolls.
options: Help her type faster
Have her stop the airplane or wait; set up nav and com before taxi
Let her; it saves time in the run-up
Take the tablet away for the flight
steps.why: Setting up radios and navigation on the roll is a leading cause of heads-down taxi; do it before taxi [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.3]].

steps.s: Climbing out, her father asks what the river below is called, and she turns to answer.
options: Answer for her
Let them chat; it is VFR
Prompt her to fly first and hold the talk until clear of the local airspace
Take the controls and say nothing
steps.why: The PHAK sterile period runs from departure to the first intermediate altitude and clear of the local airspace [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; teach the PIC to say when talk must wait [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

steps.s: In cruise she wants to fly direct to a new destination. The GPS shows a database expired last month.
options: Follow the magenta line
Verify the route and waypoints with a current sectional or Chart Supplement before relying on it
Turn off the GPS for good
Climb higher to fix it
steps.why: With an outdated database, verify waypoints using current products and do not rely on the moving map near critical airspace [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]] [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]].
